fixes.explanation: That's the voice. Matthew says a voice from heaven said, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!” It speaks right after Jesus goes up out of the water. Beloved Son and well pleased are the words that come from heaven.

John the Baptist opens with “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.” (Matthew 3:2) To repent is to turn around, and he wants the people to do it because the kingdom is close. That's his message at the start, and it's a short one. I've seen cookie recipes with more words than that.

Priests are a fair guess, since they're tied to the temple. But the text doesn't point there. The voice spoken of through the prophet Isaiah says, “Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.” That road is for the Lord, friend, and nobody else gets named.

True. Matthew says, “His food was locusts and wild honey.” That's what the text gives for John's food. I've served some strange cookie batches in my day, but I have never once put locusts on the tray.

That's it. Matthew says, “People went out to him from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan.” Jerusalem was the big city, and they still went out to the wilderness. I've had folks skip my bakery over a little rain, so this is impressive.

Matthew never names any shepherds or Bethlehem here, friend. The text says people went out to John “…from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan.” Those are the places it names.

Traders are a fun picture, but they aren't in this verse. Matthew says, “People went out to him from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan.” Those are the places he names, and Tyre isn't one of them.

True. Matthew says, “Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River.” They aren't just getting wet, friend. They're confessing their sins as they're baptized. I think that takes real nerve.

It's actually true. Matthew 3:6 says, “Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River.” The baptizing and the confessing happen together. Owning up isn't easy, so I'm proud of every one of them.
Fruit is the word. John says, “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance.” He's calling for fruit that fits with repentance. That's the word John picks, friend.
Prayers are good, friend, but they aren't the word here. John says, “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance.” He's asking for something that shows. Fruit is what he calls for.

Stones, friend. John says, “For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham.” I think that landed hard. If God can do that with rocks, nobody gets to lean on their family name.

John doesn't leave that tree standing. He says, “…every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” The axe lies ready at the root of the trees. Cut down and thrown into the fire is the picture for those trees.

Sandals, yes. John says the One coming is “…One more powerful than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.” John says he isn't even worthy of that. I think that tells you how highly he thinks of the One coming.

Pouring water on hands sounds like something a servant would do. But John doesn't say it. He says of the One coming, “…whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.” Sandals are what he names, and he says he isn't worthy to carry them.

Thorns aren't in John's picture, friend. He describes the coming One's threshing floor, where the wheat is gathered into the barn. He says, “…He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.” Chaff is what gets burned there.

Branches sound close, friend, since John also talks about trees a few verses back (Matthew 3:10). But this picture is about harvest. John says the wheat gets gathered into the barn, “but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

Blessed is a good word, friend, but it isn't the one Matthew uses. He says Jesus “…came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John.” Baptism is what the trip is for. That's the word to hold onto.
John doesn't tell Jesus to go anywhere. He tries to prevent Him, saying, “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?” I think he's surprised. Galilee never comes up in his words.
An angel is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't who Matthew names. Matthew says Jesus “…saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him.” That's who comes down.
Elijah isn't named anywhere in this scene, friend. Matthew says Jesus “…saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him.” The Spirit of God is who Jesus sees.
